national.headline: After the pandemic, remote and hybrid work pulled demand out of the office sector. Vacancy rose to record levels while property values and tax bases came under pressure — unevenly, across cities and building classes.

sf.headline: San Francisco became the poster child for empty towers and distressed pricing. Brokerage data show sustained high vacancy; policy reports (SPUR) argue recovery is long without conversion, tax reform, and downtown activation.

nyc.headline: New York's market splits: trophy Class A assets and selective leasing can stabilize headlines while Class B/C stock and fiscal exposure still matter. The NYC Comptroller frames the tension as doom loop vs. boom loop.

dc.headline: Washington, D.C. depends heavily on federal-adjacent office demand. The D.C. Office of Revenue Analysis ties rising vacant stock to valuation and property-tax risk — a fiscal Achilles' heel.

caseStudy.title: Mini case study: SF office-to-residential conversion
caseStudy.body: When a tech tenant vacates a 1960s tower at a distressed basis, the owner faces a choice: hold for years of negative cash flow or sell to a conversion specialist. Public reporting on projects like 550 California Street shows how a discounted office sale can become housing supply — the seller exits a losing asset, the buyer captures rezoning upside, and the city stabilizes a shrinking tax base. That is the "who wins" story hiding inside SF's vacancy spike.

winners: Institutional investors and well-capitalized buyers acquiring distressed or discounted assets
Owners of Class A / trophy buildings in prime locations (relative resilience)
Asset managers with long horizons who can wait out lease rollover and repricing
losers: Small businesses in downtown corridors tied to office foot traffic
Urban workers in office-adjacent services when attendance and hiring slow
Municipal budgets when assessed values and transaction volume weaken
next: Office-to-residential conversion (where economically and legally feasible)
A wall of CRE debt maturities and refinancing under higher rates
Fiscal feedback loops: weaker downtowns → fewer services → harder recovery
